program_meta.program_name: Ph.D. in Computer Science & Engineering, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle.
program_meta.degree_target: PhD (direct-admit; no separate MS-first route through this application)
program_meta.sop_limit: NO LIMIT STATED. Allen School 'How to Apply' page, VERBATIM (Personal Statement section): 'There are no requirements for length or formatting; you may be as descriptive as you would like and may utilize more than one page.' The page also calls this document by two names interchangeably: 'Personal Statement (sometimes referred to as a statement of purpose, or "the essay")'.
program_meta.extra_essays: Only one essay total (the Personal Statement above) - there is no separate diversity/personal-history statement as a distinct document at UW CSE (contrast with Berkeley/Purdue/Michigan). Required PROMPT, VERBATIM: 'Submit a personal statement of that includes: a) how you became interested in doing research, b) a relevant project or research experience that shows your technical knowledge and skill, and c) your plans for the future in computer science. You may wish to include information about what you feel are the strengths of your application, such as special interests and abilities, or give explanations for what you feel are any weaknesses in your academic record. If you have background that might particularly contribute to the intellectual and social enrichment of the program, please describe it. Examples include unique educational or cultural opportunities (or lack of them), social and economic disadvantages that you may have had to overcome, and interesting or unusual influences on your intellectual development.' Also required, per How to Apply page: a resume/CV ('no requirements for length or formatting'), and short-answer Supplemental Questions in the portal - VERBATIM: 'List keywords of research areas/topics that you are interested in. We strongly encourage you to consider using keywords your faculty of interest list in their profiles on our website.' Plus 'In 300 characters or less summarize your research experience' and 'In 300 characters or less summarize awards and other recognition you've achieved.'
program_meta.deadline_fall_2027: December 15 (Ph.D. FAQ, VERBATIM: 'What is the application deadline? December 15, with students expected to enroll in the following autumn.'). How to Apply page, VERBATIM: 'must be received by December 15th (or the next business day if the 15th falls on a weekend) at 11:59pm, Pacific Time.' -> for Fall 2027 this is December 15, 2026 (a Tuesday, so no shift). Exact Fall-2027-labeled confirmation was not separately republished at time of check - flag as Medium confidence pending the cycle's application portal opening (usually ~Sept).
program_meta.lor_count: Three (3), from all applicants. How to Apply page, VERBATIM: 'Three letters are required from all applicants. The best folks to write letters of recommendation are those people who can speak to your demonstrated research potential with specific details about the work you've done... It is not recommended to use personal references that can't speak to your demonstrated research potential.'
program_meta.gre: NOT accepted / not required. Ph.D. FAQ, VERBATIM: 'Is the GRE required? GRE scores are no longer required or accepted for the Ph.D. program. GRE scores will not be reviewed or considered by the Allen School, even if they are submitted to the University of Washington.'
program_meta.english_test: REQUIRED, NO INDIA EXEMPTION FOUND. UW Graduate School minimum scores (per FAQ table): TOEFL iBT 80 to apply / 92+ preferred ('ELP Satisfied'); IELTS 6.5 to apply / 7.0+ preferred; Duolingo 105 to apply / 120+ preferred. Waiver routes are based on prior DEGREE and medium-of-instruction (Graduate Policy 3.2), not citizenship/country: 'A bachelor's, master's or doctoral degree from a regionally accredited institution located in the United States and where English is the medium of instruction' or an equivalent non-US institution where English is the sole medium of instruction - India is not listed as a blanket-exempt country the way it is at UT Austin. Akshat would need his undergraduate institution to certify English-medium instruction to attempt a waiver; otherwise a TOEFL/IELTS/Duolingo score is required. NOT VERIFIED this pass: whether Allen School sets a higher department-specific bar than the university minimum (common at peer schools) - flag as a gap.
program_meta.app_fee: $90.00 USD (UW Graduate School 'Apply Now' page, VERBATIM: 'The nonrefundable application fee is $90.00 (USD) or $75.00 for Graduate Non-Matriculated applications.'). Fee waivers exist only for U.S. residents demonstrating financial need (Graduate School page) - international applicants are NOT eligible per that same page.

program_meta.advisor_model: ADMITTED TO THE DEPARTMENT, NOT TO A SPECIFIC ADVISOR - no formal rotation system. Ph.D. FAQ, VERBATIM: 'Do I need to secure a faculty advisor before applying? ... You do not need to contact faculty prior to applying, nor is it expected.' Applicants may name up to 3 research interest areas and, optionally, specific faculty names in a supplemental question - VERBATIM: 'If you are confident that you'd like to work with any particular faculty member(s), you may indicate their name(s) in the supplemental question. This question is optional but is strongly encouraged to make sure your application is reviewed by the appropriate reviewers during the admissions process.' Admissions committee is holistic/school-wide; students then arrange advising after arrival (norms vary lab to lab - some faculty explicitly invite pre-admission contact regardless of the school-wide default, e.g. Su-In Lee's lab page and Simon Du's homepage both solicit direct emails from prospective students).
program_meta.ms_research_access: NO STANDALONE FULL-TIME RESEARCH MS EXISTS - this is a defining UW CSE quirk. Ph.D. FAQ, VERBATIM: 'Do you have a master's program? [Allen School] does not offer a standalone, full-time master's program; rather, the part-time, evening Professional Master's Program is the only MS program available. The PMP is a coursework-based program designed for fully employed software developers residing in the Seattle area at the time of application. To be considered for admission, an applicant must have a minimum of two years of full-time, post-degree professional software [experience].' The PMP is explicitly NOT a research/thesis degree and is closed to applicants without professional work history, so it is not a viable lab-access route for Akshat. Consequence: at UW, the ONLY way to get into Allen School labs as a masters-oriented applicant would be a PhD admit who later masters-out, or affiliation through another UW graduate program (e.g., a research MS in ECE or an interdisciplinary program) with a CSE-affiliated advisor - not verified this pass.
program_meta.notes: INTERVIEW / CONTACT QUIRKS: no explicit 'we do not do interviews' statement was found on the public FAQ/How-to-Apply pages this pass (flag as gap, not confirmed absent). The strongest concrete quirk found is the advisor-model language above ('you do not need to contact faculty ... nor is it expected'), which functions similarly to a soft do-not-cold-email norm at the SCHOOL level, though individual faculty override it (Su-In Lee, Simon Du explicitly invite emails; Ranjay Krishna/Ali Farhadi's RAIVN lab requires a form + email to the 'most relevant person'). TAship requirement: Ph.D. students must TA at least two quarters, satisfied via an English test, an appeal interview, or ENGL 105 (English for International Teaching Assistants) - the only place the word 'interview' appears in the FAQ, and it is about TA English certification, not admissions. FUNDING: Ph.D. FAQ states the school funds every admitted PhD student (RA/TA/fellowship) - exact guarantee language not fully captured this pass, flag Medium confidence. CROSS-UNIT CAVEAT: several strong faculty matches (Su-In Lee, Sewoong Oh, Simon Du, Kevin Jamieson, Pang Wei Koh) are core Allen School CS faculty reachable via this single application; others of interest (e.g., Ani Kembhavi, formerly AI2) hold only an Affiliate/Adjunct appointment and are NOT full CS faculty who admit PhD students through this process. GAPS: (1) Department-specific English-score bar (if any) above the university minimum not found. (2) Whether Fall-2027-specific deadline text has been separately republished not confirmed (using the standing 'December 15' rule). (3) e-Science Institute and AI2 formal-affiliate lists were not systematically enumerated this pass - only individuals already named in the brief were checked.

faculty.department: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
faculty.lab: No separately named lab; group listed on personal homepage. Co-affiliated with UW ML and NLP groups.
faculty.research_areas: Data-centric ML and foundation models: dataset curation/selection for pretraining (DataComp, DataComp-LM, DataDecide), influence functions and distributional robustness, reliability of AI systems, AI for science.
faculty.why_match: Koh's DataComp-LM (NeurIPS 2024 D&B Track) and DataDecide (ICML 2025) treat the training set itself as the object of controlled experimentation - fixing the model and ablating only the data pipeline to isolate what data choices actually contribute to downstream performance, exactly the ablation logic Akshat used in his U-Net variant benchmarking (lung segmentation) and polyp preprocessing study, where he showed preprocessing gains shrink as architecture strengthens. Koh's 'Using unlabeled data to enhance fairness of medical AI' (Nature Medicine 2024) also connects directly to Akshat's label-scarcity thread (semi-supervised spine MRI pseudo-labeling with MC-dropout uncertainty filtering).
faculty.key_paper_1: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models. NeurIPS (Datasets and Benchmarks Track), 2024.
faculty.key_paper_2: DataDecide: How to predict best pretraining data with small experiments. ICML, 2025. (See also: Using unlabeled data to enhance fairness of medical AI, Nature Medicine 2024.)
faculty.taking_students: Yes. Homepage, VERBATIM: 'I am recruiting for the 2025-2026 cycle and am looking for students and postdocs who are doing core ML/NLP research and/or are interested in AI for science broadly construed.' Cycle label not yet updated to 2026-2027 at time of check - re-verify closer to application time. Verified 2026-08-28.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'If you are interested in joining us, please read this [link]' - points to general prospective-student guidance rather than a strict do-not-email rule. No explicit prohibition found.
faculty.email_angle: My polyp-segmentation ablations showed preprocessing gains shrink as the architecture gets stronger - the same 'what does the data actually buy you' question your DataComp-LM/DataDecide work asks at pretraining scale, and I'd like to work on that question with real label constraints instead of synthetic ablations.
faculty.notes: Also holds a part-time industry role as Member of Technical Staff, Microsoft AI (works on the OLMo/Olmo 3 line jointly with AI2/UW collaborators) - not a red flag by itself since his UW lab is clearly active with many current PhD students, but note the dual affiliation.

faculty.department: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering (Adjunct, Department of Statistics)
faculty.lab: No separately named lab; group page at homepage lists current advisees.
faculty.research_areas: Active learning and adaptive experimentation with instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees; bandits; hyperparameter optimization; closed-loop measurement design.
faculty.why_match: Jamieson's research is about deciding, in a closed loop, which future measurement is worth taking given a fixed statistical budget - the same problem Akshat solved empirically in the spine-MRI pseudo-labeling study, where per-class confidence thresholds calibrated on just 5 reference images matched thresholds derived from 304 (a calibration-efficiency result Jamieson's instance-dependent sample-complexity framework could formalize). His active-learning guarantees are also the natural theoretical lens for Akshat's open, unresolved DDPM-pretraining negative result (liver transfers, kidney doesn't) - i.e., which unlabeled examples/organs are informative to pretrain on at all.
faculty.key_paper_1: Instance-dependent sample complexity bounds for active learning / pure-exploration bandits (representative theme across his COLT/NeurIPS body of work - see homepage publications list for current titles).
faculty.key_paper_2: Group publications on adaptive experimentation and hyperparameter optimization (see https://jamieson.people.washington.edu/publications.html for current entries).
faculty.scholar: not captured this pass - see homepage links
faculty.taking_students: Yes. Homepage banner, VERBATIM: 'Now recruiting graduate students and post-docs! Please read more here.' Verified 2026-08-28.
faculty.contact_policy: Not stated beyond the recruiting banner linking to further instructions (not fetched in full this pass) - treat as an open door pending that page's detail; do not assume unrestricted.
faculty.email_angle: My spine-MRI pseudo-labeling work found that per-class confidence thresholds calibrated on 5 reference images matched thresholds derived from 304 - a calibration-efficiency result I only showed empirically, and I'd like to understand it through the instance-dependent sample-complexity lens your active-learning work provides.
faculty.notes: Strong methodological fit but no direct medical-imaging or generative-model history found this pass - the connection is at the level of 'sample/measurement efficiency under a budget,' not domain overlap. faculty.department: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
faculty.research_areas: Explainable AI (originated SHAP), interpretable/controllable foundation models applied to computational biology, medicine, and healthcare; multi-omic, imaging, clinical, and text data.
faculty.why_match: Lee's lab treats interpretability and uncertainty as first-class outputs of a biomedical AI system, not an afterthought - the same posture behind Akshat's A-PDF work, where a post-hoc distributional-plausibility filter (not the GAN discriminator itself) is trusted to decide which synthetic masks are anatomically real. Her XAI machinery (SHAP and successors) is a natural fit for auditing exactly the kind of frozen-encoder failure Akshat found in his DDPM-pretraining work (kidney transfer fails, worse than random init) - a case where knowing WHY the encoder fails matters as much as knowing THAT it fails.
faculty.key_paper_1: SHAP and related explainable-AI framework papers (foundational; see lab publications page for the current canonical citation).
faculty.key_paper_2: Current AIMS Lab publications on interpretable/controllable foundation models for computational biology and medicine (see https://suinlee.cs.washington.edu/publications for up-to-date titles).
faculty.scholar: not captured this pass - see lab site
faculty.taking_students: Unstated directly as Yes/No, but the lab actively manages a prospective-PhD-applicant workflow (see contact policy) implying she does admit students most cycles - verify current-cycle status directly.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM, from the AIMS Lab Jobs page: 'Please note that Prof. Lee receives a very large volume of emails from prospective Ph.D. applicants interested in the AIMS Lab and is unable to reply to most inquiries. faculty.department: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
faculty.research_areas: Theoretical machine learning: reinforcement learning theory, non-convex optimization, representation learning guarantees, data synthesis and selection, test-time compute.
faculty.why_match: Du's 'Few-Shot Learning via Learning the Representation, Provably' formalizes exactly the empirical question behind Akshat's DDPM-pretraining transfer study - under what conditions does a learned representation transfer to a new task, and why does it fail (kidney) when it succeeds elsewhere (liver)? The connection is theoretical grounding for an empirical negative result Akshat currently only has data on, not an existing methods overlap.
faculty.key_paper_1: Few-Shot Learning via Learning the Representation, Provably. ICLR, 2021.
faculty.key_paper_2: Is a Good Representation Sufficient for Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning? ICLR, 2020.
